rule: decision 47: a mapping the blind verifier did not confirm is held — never shown, never a diagnosis, never S5 evidence — until a human keeps or drops it

items.stem: Box A contains 3 cards numbered 1, 2 and 3. Box B contains 2 cards numbered 1 and 2. One card is removed at random from each box. Build the sample space: tap every outcome (card from Box A, card from Box B) that could happen.
items.construction: X = Box A = [1,2,3], Y = Box B = [1,2] (both within the 2-4 number limit). Tap all six ordered pairs of X x Y: (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2), (3,1), (3,2), and none of the decoys (such as reversed pairs like (1,3) or (2,3), which are impossible because Box B has no card 3).
items.predicate_meaning: An incomplete product: some pairs of X×Y were not selected
items.misconception_label: Gives an event in place of the sample space
items.misconception_description: The student writes a set picked out by a condition, such as only the odd numbers on a die, when the sample space is every possible outcome of the experiment.
items.why: The instrument can emit missing-pairs for this question, and it fires whenever any of the six pairs is left untapped. But the question states no event or condition, so there is nothing for a student to filter on. A student who confuses an event with the sample space has no condition to apply here. Leaving pairs out in this widget is far more likely to come from forgetting some combinations, pairing the cards one-to-one (only (1,1) and (2,2)), or treating (1,2) and (2,1) as the same outcome. The predicate would mostly fire for those reasons rather than for sample-space-as-an-event, so the diagnosis would refute a mistake the student did not make.

items.stem: Two dice are rolled and you hope for a total of 8. The grid shows every possible outcome as (first die, second die). Tap every outcome that belongs to the event "the total is 8".
items.construction: Instrument: 6x6 grid with rule {kind:sum, op:eq, value:8}, within the 2-8 limits for rows and cols. The student taps the five cells whose two dice add to 8: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2). n(E)=5, n(S)=36. The event is non-empty and the rule produces exactly these cells, so the question can be answered correctly on this instrument.
items.predicate_meaning: Counted a compound outcome once where the grid shows several ways to make it
items.misconception_label: Lists only some of the outcomes that give the wanted result
items.misconception_description: The student writes down one or two outcomes that give the wanted result, such as a total of 8, and treats that as the whole event set, leaving out the other outcomes that also give it.
items.why: This predicate fires when ordered pairs are collapsed, so a student picks (3,5) but not (5,3), or (2,6) but not (6,2). That is an order-matters or unordered-pair error, not the claimed one. The claimed misconception is stopping after one or two outcomes and treating them as the whole event. A student who stops early would only incidentally trip this predicate. Most of the time it would fire because of the ordering error, so the diagnosis would be wrong.

items.stem: A club has learners who play Football ($F$) and learners who play Chess ($C$). Some play both and some play neither. The rectangle holds every learner in the club. Shade the complement of Chess, $C'$.
items.construction: Shade exactly two regions: the Football-only region (inside the Football circle, outside the Chess circle) and the region inside the rectangle but outside both circles (neither). Leave the whole Chess circle unshaded, meaning both the Chess-only lens and the Football-and-Chess overlap. This is everything in the rectangle that is not in Chess, which is C'.
items.predicate_meaning: Wrong in a way none of the named errors describes
items.misconception_label: Complement is only what lies outside every circle
items.misconception_description: The student takes the complement of a single event to be just the numbers that sit outside all the circles in the diagram, so numbers that are in the other circle but not in the event get left out.
items.why: off-target is the residual predicate for any wrong shading that no named predicate describes. The claimed misconception does produce one such shading: only the neither region shaded, with Football-only left out. That shading fires neither complement-inside-a nor neither-region-missed, so it falls into off-target. But off-target fires equally for many other wrong builds: the whole Football circle, the complement of Football instead (Chess-only plus neither), the union, the intersection, or a random region. A student who shaded the Football circle because she thinks the complement of Chess is the other set has not made the 'only outside every circle' mistake. Pinning that specific refutation on a catch-all predicate would show it to students who did not make that mistake, so the diagnosis does not match.
